transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-12-10
Time: 15:00 EST
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Li (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (CISO, Glacier Bank), Priya Desai (Cloud Architect), Evan Torres (Security Engineer)

Summary:
Redwood gives a technical deep dive on Private/VPC deployment security architecture. Focus areas: network isolation, ingress/egress patterns, firewalling, RBAC/SSO integration, audit logs and retention, KMS/encryption at rest and transit, SOC 2/ISO evidence. Customer clarifies data residency and strict egress controls; requests network diagrams, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and a pilot plan.

Topics Covered:
- Private deployment overview and control plane options
- VPC networking: peering, TGW, and transit flows
- Ingress: load balancer vs direct peering, allowed sources
- Egress: firewalling, NAT, restricted outbound endpoints
- Firewalling & security groups: host vs network layer rules
- RBAC, SSO/SAML, provisioning, SCIM
- Audit logs, retention, integrity, and SIEM forwarding
- Encryption: KMS, customer-managed keys, HSM integrations
- Compliance artifacts: SOC 2/ISO27001, pen test reports

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the network diagram and threat model.
[00:18] Daniel Kim: Yep hi, Daniel here. We're mainly interested in private deployment options and ensuring we can meet our egress policies and SOC 2 requirements.
[00:25] Marco Li: Great; I'm Marco, I'll take the deep network and infra questions. Just to set expectations, we'll cover VPC peering patterns, ingress/egress options, and how we integrate with customer KMS and audit pipelines.
[00:40] Priya Desai: Sounds good. Our main constraints: data residency in US-east only, no public internet egress except to like specific S3 endpoints and our SIEM.
[00:50] Evan Torres: And we need RBAC tied to our SSO, with SCIM provisioning, also want to understand audit log schemas and retention options.

[01:05] Marco Li: Ok. High level, Redwood Private gives you a control plane that can be run either in Redwood's managed control plane with a customer VPC peering, or a fully customer-managed control plane in your VPC or on-prem. For Glacier Bank you told us you need network isolation and restricted egress — so we typically recommend the VPC-hosted control plane with private peering + transit gateway for cross-AZ traffic.
[01:35] Daniel Kim: When you say peering, are we talking simple VPC peering or do you recommend a transit gateway? We have multiple account structure — prod, staging, data plane in separate accounts.
[01:48] Marco Li: Good question. For multiple accounts and central egress controls we prefer a Transit Gateway (TGW) or AWS Network Firewall in the central network account. Peering scales poorly across many accounts. With TGW you can centralize egress inspection and route tables.
[02:05] Priya Desai: And can we force all egress to go through our outbound proxy and the firewall? No direct internet.
[02:12] Marco Li: Yes, you can. Deployment options let you terminate egress at a NAT/egress VPC controlled by Glacier Bank. Redwood's serving nodes communicate outbound only to configured endpoints — for example S3, KMS endpoints, and Redwood's private control endpoints — and you can block anything else at the firewall/NAT.

[02:40] Evan Torres: How about load balancing for ingress — we can't expose a public ELB. We want internal ELB + peering.
[02:46] Marco Li: Internal ALB/NLB inside the customer's VPC is typical. Requests from your application reach Redwood's private endpoints over the TGW/VPC peering. If you want zero-trust, you can also do mutual TLS between your services and Redwood collectors.
[03:05] Aisha Patel: I'll note mTLS as an option — we have a reference doc for mTLS + VPC peering, I'll share the link after.

[03:20] Daniel Kim: On encryption — we require CMEK, customer-managed keys. Do you support BYOK and HSM-backed keys?
[03:27] Marco Li: Yes. For Private we support customer-managed KMS keys. You can either give Redwood a key policy in your account or we can integrate with your KMS via a cross-account role. For HSM-backed keys we can work with an external HSM if you need FIPS-level controls, there's an integration pattern we can share.
[03:45] Priya Desai: So the model artifacts and KV cache — is that encrypted at rest with our KMS?
[03:50] Marco Li: Everything stored in persistent storage in your VPC is encrypted using your CMEK. The KV cache in-memory isn't persisted unless you snapshot; snapshots are written encrypted.

[04:05] Evan Torres: Audit logging — we need immutable logs shipped to our SIEM with at least 7 years retention, integrity protection, and tamper-evidence. How does that work?
[04:15] Marco Li: Redwood can stream audit events — auth events, request metadata, model version, and admin actions — to customer destinations (Kinesis/Firehose/S3) in real time. We also support write-once S3 buckets with Object Lock for tamper protection if you enable it and configure bucket policies. Retention policy is enforced on your side.
[04:35] Daniel Kim: Can we get hashed request content in logs? We can't have raw PII in logs.
[04:40] Marco Li: Yes, we support configurable PII redaction and hashing at the ingestion point. You can also route full request bodies to a restricted bucket with tighter access controls if you need full fidelity for audits.

[05:00] Priya Desai: Regarding RBAC and SSO, we want SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO mapped to our groups. Is there an admin hierarchy and fine-grained role controls?
[05:10] Marco Li: Yes. Redwood's RBAC supports organization roles, team roles, and resource-level permissions. We map SAML assertions to roles, and SCIM provisioning creates accounts with initial group membership. Admins can set per-route and per-model permissions.
[05:30] Aisha Patel: I'll follow up with a schema doc showing available RBAC roles and example SAML mappings.

[05:42] Evan Torres: Network egress to external model registries — do you call out to external registries by default? We want to ensure no outbound calls to third-party registries during normal operation.
[05:50] Marco Li: By default in Private mode we avoid external registry pulls unless you enable model downloads from public registries. If you want completely air-gapped operation we can package models into a tarball and load them from your internal artifact repo.

[06:10] Daniel Kim: Pen testing and compliance: do you provide SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 certs? Also, do you do third-party pen tests and share findings?
[06:20] Aisha Patel: We do provide SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 reports for our managed offerings; for Private deployments we provide evidence and an artifacts pack. We also have third-party pen test summaries and redacted reports we can share under NDA.
[06:35] Priya Desai: Can we get network diagrams for the private deployment that show control plane connectivity, ingress, and egress paths?
[06:41] Marco Li: Yes, we have template diagrams. We'll customize them to reflect TGW, peering, and your central firewall.

[06:55] Daniel Kim: One more — do you integrate with our KMS for envelope encryption for model weights and also for tokenization caches?
[07:05] Marco Li: We do envelope encryption for artifacts stored to object storage; for token caches you can choose to persist them encrypted with CMEK or keep them ephemeral in-memory.

[07:20] Evan Torres: Regarding firewalling: what's the recommended security group layout and host OS hardening for the serving nodes?
[07:27] Marco Li: We recommend a minimal host security group that only allows traffic from the control-plane subnets and health check endpoints. At the host level we run a hardened AMI with CIS benchmarks where applicable; for on-prem we provide a baseline config.

[07:45] Priya Desai: Do you support network policies for pod-level segmentation if we run on EKS?
[07:51] Marco Li: Yes, we support Calico and AWS Security Groups for pods via the AWS VPC CNI; we can provide manifest examples for policy enforcement.

[08:05] Aisha Patel: Quick question for timeline — what would the pilot look like? Marco, maybe outline the steps.
[08:12] Marco Li: Pilot typically: 1) exchange network ranges and IAM roles, 2) deploy control plane in a staging VPC or enable peering, 3) deploy a small 2-4 GPU data plane, 4) run connectivity and benchmark tests, 5) validate audit streaming and RBAC. Should be 2-3 weeks depending on approvals.
[08:35] Daniel Kim: Approvals are an issue but doable. We'll need a clear checklist for our infra team.

[09:00] Evan Torres: About egress filtering — do you provide a deny-by-default policy and only allow specific endpoints?
[09:06] Marco Li: Yes, our recommended posture is deny-by-default with allow-lists for S3 endpoints, KMS, and Redwood control endpoints. We provide a sample security group and network ACL template.

[09:25] Priya Desai: Any special handling for secrets and environment variables in the data plane?
[09:30] Marco Li: We integrate with your secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager/HashiCorp Vault) and avoid storing plaintext secrets. Injection is done at startup via IAM roles and KMS-decryption.

[09:50] Daniel Kim: For SIEM integration, what fields are in the audit schema? We need IP, user ID, action, model version, request hash, timestamp, and request route.
[09:59] Marco Li: Correct — we include those fields plus response token count, latency, and model checksum. We can add custom fields if you have a specific schema.

[10:20] Aisha Patel: Going to show a short example network flow diagram — sharing screen now.
[10:30] [screen share walkthrough, minor audio overlap, some words garbled]
[11:00] Marco Li: So here's the TGW in the network account, your central firewall, and the Redwood data plane in your private subnets. Routes send all outbound to the firewall. Health checks go to a dedicated monitoring VPC.

[11:30] Priya Desai: This visual helps. About DNS — we want internal-only DNS names.
[11:35] Marco Li: You can host private hosted zones in Route53 or your own DNS. We support customizing the endpoint domain.

[12:00] Evan Torres: Are there any managed NAT gateways we need to be careful about from a compliance perspective?
[12:06] Marco Li: You control NAT gateways for egress; we suggest a central NAT with proxy and egress inspection rather than per-AZ NATs to centralize logging.

[12:25] Daniel Kim: On application-level data handling — can you provide a data flow that shows where PII is masked and logs hashed?
[12:32] Marco Li: Yes, our ingestion pipeline supports redaction rules. We'll send a sample rule set.

[12:50] Priya Desai: For the control plane, do you require any inbound rules from Redwood to our VPC?
[12:56] Marco Li: Only for the initial peering and control channel — we recommend a single ingress CIDR from Redwood control IPs, over TLS, and you can lock it to specific ports.

[13:15] Aisha Patel: I'll capture that as an action item: provide control plane IPs and recommended SGs.

[13:25] Evan Torres: What's your approach to vulnerability scanning on the data plane images?
[13:30] Marco Li: We run automated CVE scanning on images, publish SBOMs, and can run scheduled patching windows in consultation with your team. For air-gapped installs we provide patched image bundles.

[13:55] Daniel Kim: Ok good. On legal/compliance — will we need a Data Processing Agreement and addendum for data residency?
[14:02] Aisha Patel: Yes, we have a DPA and data residency addendum; we'll attach them in the follow-up.

[14:20] Priya Desai: For long-term retention of logs — you mentioned Object Lock. Will Redwood manage the lifecycle or does Glacier Bank manage it?
[14:27] Marco Li: For Private, logs land in your bucket so you set Object Lock and lifecycle. Redwood will write with limited access so we can't delete locked objects.

[14:45] Evan Torres: Any thoughts on third-party penetration tests for the combined deployment? We might want an engagement that tests both infra and integration points.
[14:54] Marco Li: We can coordinate a joint pen test; there are standard scopes we recommend. We'll provide a template statement of work.

[15:10] Daniel Kim: Are there any default telemetry endpoints we need to whitelist?
[15:15] Marco Li: Only our control-plane endpoints and optional telemetry sinks you enable; list will be provided.

[15:35] Aisha Patel: I'm going to quickly cover the compliance artifacts we'll send: SOC 2 Type II report (redacted), ISO27001 certificate, pen test summary, red-team findings, and RBAC schema.
[15:50] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[16:05] [small crosstalk and a brief pause as attendees check links]

[16:20] Evan Torres: One last deep question — how do you protect against lateral movement if a single serving node is compromised?
[16:28] Marco Li: Isolation is multi-layered: host-level hardening, sec groups with least-privilege, pod/network policies, and encrypted communication. We also run runtime detection and can isolate nodes automatically by removing them from the TGW routing table if suspicious activity is detected.

[16:55] Daniel Kim: That automatic isolation sounds useful — any false-positive rates you've seen?
[17:00] Marco Li: Sorry — little garble — we tune thresholds with you; false positives are rare but we provide manual override.

[17:20] Priya Desai: Ok. Let's talk timing — we'll aim for a December pilot start if we can get approvals this week.

[17:30] Aisha Patel: Great. Recap of action items: we'll send SOC2/ISO artifacts, network diagrams, VPC peering checklist, RBAC schema, and a pilot plan. Marco will prepare the technical templates. Evan will send CIDR ranges.

[17:55] Daniel Kim: Yes I'll send the CIDRs and primary contacts by Wednesday.

[18:10] Aisha Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: speaker attribution has a few mislabels and occasional garbled words; audio overlap during screen share produced some transcription noise.
